questions.stem: Soup cools according to \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-21)\), where k is positive. Initially \(T(0)=96^circ C\). Show that \(T=21+75e^{-kt}\) is a solution.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Differentiating gives \(dT/dt=-75ke^{-kt}\). Also \(-k(T-21)=-k(75e^{-kt})=-75ke^{-kt}\), so the proposed function satisfies the differential equation. At t=0, \(T=21+75=96\), so it also satisfies the initial condition.
questions.hint: Differentiate the proposed temperature function and separately substitute it into the right side of the differential equation.

keyPoints.note: Differentiate the exponential term using the chain rule.
Check the initial condition after checking the differential equation.

steps.explain: Differentiate the proposed solution with respect to time.
Substitute the proposed solution into the right side of the differential equation.
Both sides agree, and the initial value is correct.

questions.stem: \(N\) is the number of finches in a certain population at time \(t\) years. The population size \(N\) satisfies the equation \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=-k(N-1500)\), for some constant \(k\). Verify that \(N=1500+Ae^{-kt}\) (where \(A\) is a constant) is a solution of the equation \(\dfrac{dN}{dt}=-k(N-1500)\). Which working correctly verifies this?
questions.hint: Differentiate \(N=1500+Ae^{-kt}\) (the derivative of the constant 1500 is 0), then rewrite \(Ae^{-kt}\) as \(N-1500\).

steps.explain: Start with the proposed solution and differentiate with respect to \(t\). The derivative of a constant (1500) is 0, and \(\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{-kt}=-ke^{-kt}\) (chain rule: multiply by the derivative \(-k\) of the power).
Now express the right-hand side of the differential equation. From \(N=1500+Ae^{-kt}\), subtract 1500: \(N-1500=Ae^{-kt}\).
Substitute \(Ae^{-kt}=N-1500\) into the derivative.
This is exactly the given equation, so \(N=1500+Ae^{-kt}\) is a solution for any constant \(A\) ✓.
Why not the others: B has the wrong sign (the derivative of \(e^{-kt}\) is NEGATIVE); C replaces \(Ae^{-kt}\) by \(N\) instead of \(N-1500\); D thinks the derivative of 1500 is 1500 (it is 0).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Differentiate, then replace A e to the minus kt by N minus 1500.

questions.stem: The direction field below represents one of these differential equations. Which equation matches the field?
questions.hint: Look for where the direction segments are horizontal (slope 0), then where they are vertical (undefined).

keyPoints.note: A horizontal short segment indicates \(dy/dx=0\); vertical segments indicate an undefined slope.

steps.explain: In the supplied field, horizontal segments lie along the diagonal through the origin with positive gradient about 2. That means the numerator must vanish when \(y=2x\).
The near-vertical segments occur on the line \(2y-x=0\), so this expression belongs in the denominator.
Combine the numerator and denominator identified from the field.

questions.hint: Check where the slopes are horizontal and where the slope changes sign.

steps.explain: Look at simple places first. Along the \(y\)-axis (\(x=0\)) the segments are horizontal, so \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\) when \(x=0\). That rules out B and D (they are undefined at \(x=0\)).
Next compare signs. At \((2,1)\) the slope is positive, but at \((2,-1)\) (below the \(x\)-axis) it is negative. So the sign of \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) changes when \(y\) changes sign.

steps.explain: Find where the segments are vertical: along \(y=x\). There \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) is undefined, so the denominator is \(x-y\) or \(y-x\).
Decide the sign with one point, e.g. \((1,0)\) on the positive \(x\)-axis, where the slope is positive (segments go up to the right).
So the equation is \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y}{x-y}\), option A.

keyPoints.text: Which of the following could be the differential equation represented?
keyPoints.note: Slope 0 along y = −x and vertical along y = x; test (1, 0) for the sign.

questions.stem: Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=y^2\cos x\), given \(y(\pi/6)=-\frac{1}{2}\).
questions.hint: Separate the y and x terms, integrate, and use the initial condition to find the constant.

keyPoints.note: Move (1/y^2) beside dy and (\cos x) beside dx.
Use this value after integrating to determine the constant.

steps.explain: Separate variables.
Integrate both sides.
Substitute \(x=\pi/6, y=-1/2\).
Rearrange for y.

questions.stem: Find the particular solutions to the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2x-1}{y^2}\) given \(y=\sqrt[3]{3}\) when \(x=0\).
questions.hint: Separate: ∫y² dy = ∫(2x − 1) dx, then find c from the initial value.

steps.explain: Separate the variables.
Solve for \(y\).

keyPoints.note: Separate variables, integrate, then substitute x = 0, y = ∛3 to find c.

questions.stem: A solution to the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{\cos(x+y)+\cos(x-y)}\) can be obtained from:
questions.hint: Expand cos(x + y) + cos(x − y) = 2cos x cos y, then separate.

steps.explain: Expand both cosines with the compound angle formulas.
steps.work: \(\cos(x+y)+\cos(x-y)=(\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y)+(\cos x\cos y+\sin x\sin y)=2\cos x\cos y\)

steps.explain: Simplify the differential equation.
Separate the variables: multiply by \(\cos y\) and by \(dx\).
Integrate both sides: option A.

keyPoints.note: The denominator simplifies to 2cos x cos y; then separate variables.

questions.stem: Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^2}{1+x^2}\) given \(y(0)=1\).
questions.hint: Separate: ∫y⁻² dy = ∫dx/(1 + x²). Remember ∫y⁻² dy = −1/y.

steps.explain: Separate the variables.
Integrate both sides.
Solve for \(y\).
Check: at \(x=0\), \(y=1\) ✓. Missing the minus sign from \(\int y^{-2}dy=-y^{-1}\) gives option B.

keyPoints.note: Separate variables, integrate, then use y = 1 at x = 0 to find c.

questions.stem: Solve the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{(2-y)\sqrt{2-x^2}}\) given that when \(x=1\), \(y=0\). Express \(y\) as a function of \(x\).
questions.hint: Separate, use the initial condition, complete the square in y, choose the sign using y(1) = 0.

steps.explain: Separate the variables.
Multiply by \(-2\) and complete the square in \(y\).
\(y-2=\pm\sqrt{\dots}\). At \(x=1\), \(y=0\) so \(y-2=-2\lt0\): take the negative root.
Check at \(x=1\): \(\sqrt{\frac\pi2+4-\frac\pi2}=2\), so \(y=0\) ✓.

keyPoints.note: After integrating, complete the square in y; y(1) = 0 decides the ± sign.

questions.stem: At time \(t\) seconds the length of the side of a cube is \(x\) cm, the surface area of the cube is \(S\) cm², and the volume of the cube is \(V\) cm³. The surface area of the cube is increasing at a constant rate of \(8\,\text{cm}^2\text{s}^{-1}\).
questions.hint: Connect the changing cube dimensions to S and V first. For the final part, solve the resulting separable differential equation and apply its initial condition.

keyPoints.note: This gives the value of \(dS/dt\).
Use \(S=6x^2\) for a cube.
Use \(V=x^3\) to connect volume and side length.

parts.stem: Show that \(\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{k}{x}\) where k is a constant.
parts.answer: \(S=6x², so dS/dt=12x(dx/dt)=8 and dx/dt=2/(3x); hence k=2/3.\)
parts.hint: Write the cube’s surface area in terms of x, differentiate with respect to time, and use dS/dt=8.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: A cube has six square faces, each of area x².
Differentiate with respect to t using the chain rule because x varies with time.
Insert the stated surface-area rate.
Divide by 12x and identify k.

parts.hint: Use V=x³ and substitute the rate dx/dt found in the previous part.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: Write the cube volume in terms of its side.
Differentiate with respect to time.
Substitute dx/dt=2/(3x) and simplify.
Replace x with V^(1/3), since V=x³.

parts.stem: Given that \(V=8\) when \(t=0\), solve the differential equation in part (b), and find the value of \(t\) when \(V=16\sqrt2\).
parts.hint: Separate the variables in dV/dt=2V^(1/3), integrate both sides, then use V(0)=8.

keyPoints.note: Use this initial condition after integrating to determine the constant.
Substitute this into the integrated equation and simplify its power first.

steps.explain: Separate variables.
Integrate both sides.
Use V=8 at t=0 to find C.
Rearrange to isolate V^(2/3).
Evaluate the target volume's power.
Solve and state time units.

questions.stem: For the differential equation \(y′=\frac{6}{5x^2+4x-1}\):
questions.hint: Factor the denominator, separate the partial fractions, integrate, and then apply the given point.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

parts.stem: For the differential equation \(y′=\frac{6}{5x^2+4x-1}\), show that \(y′=\frac5{5x-1}-\frac1{x+1}\).
parts.hint: Factor the denominator, then combine the proposed partial fractions over a common denominator to verify the numerator is 6.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: Factor the denominator.
Combine the proposed partial fractions over the common denominator.
Expand the numerator; the x terms cancel.
This reproduces the original derivative, proving the decomposition.

parts.stem: Find the solution to the differential equation, given that when \(x=\frac12\), \(y=3\).
parts.hint: Integrate the partial fractions, include the constant, then use the initial condition to determine it.

keyPoints.note: Focus on this information from the question when choosing the method and carrying out the calculation.

steps.explain: Integrate each term in the decomposition.
For the first term, u=5x−1 and du=5dx; integrate the second logarithm directly.
Combine logs and add the integration constant.
Substitute x=1/2,y=3 to determine C.
On the interval containing x=1/2, x>1/5 and the ratio is positive.

questions.stem: A population of 1200 feral cats is released into Darling Point. The rate of increase of the feral cat population is: \(\frac{dP}{dt}=\frac{P}{30}\left(1-\frac{P}{10000}\right)\) where \(P\) is the feral cat population and \(t\) is the number of months.

parts.hint: Combine the right-hand side over the common denominator.

steps.explain: Start from the right-hand side and use a common denominator.
Simplify the numerator.

keyPoints.note: Work from the right-hand side: common denominator P(10000 − P).

parts.stem: Hence solve the differential equation \(\frac{dP}{dt}=\frac{P}{30}\left(1-\frac{P}{10000}\right)\) for \(P\) in terms of \(t\).
parts.hint: Separate variables, integrate with (i), use P(0) = 1200, then make P the subject.

steps.explain: Rewrite and separate.
Use (i).
Solve for \(P\).

keyPoints.note: Use the partial fractions from (i): ∫(1/P + 1/(10000 − P)) dP = t/30 + c.

parts.stem: Hence find the limiting feral cat population.

steps.explain: As \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-\frac{t}{30}}\to0\).
This matches the logistic equation: growth stops when \(1-\frac{P}{10000}=0\).

parts.stem: How many months does it take for the population to double?
parts.hint: Set P = 2400 in your solution and solve for t.

steps.explain: Doubling means \(P=2400\).
Solve for \(t\).
About 25 months. (Pure exponential growth \(1200e^{t/30}\) would give \(30\ln2\approx21\) — wrong model.)

keyPoints.note: Doubling from 1200 means P = 2400.

questions.stem:
A team of biologists released 500 fish into a lake with a maximum carrying capacity of 10000 fish. It was found that the number of fish tripled during the first year. The fish population, \(N\), in the lake after \(t\) years is modelled by the logistic equation:

\(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN(10000-N)\)

where \(k\) is a constant.

parts.stem: Given \(\frac{10000}{N(10000-N)}=\frac1N+\frac{1}{10000-N}\), solve the differential equation to show that the fish population after \(t\) years is \(N=\frac{10000}{1+19e^{-10000kt}}\).
parts.hint: Separate variables, integrate with the given partial fractions, use N = 500 at t = 0.

steps.explain: Separate the variables and multiply both sides by 10000.
Integrate from \(t=0\) (\(N=500\)) using the given partial fractions.
Combine the logs and substitute the lower limit: \(\frac{500}{9500}=\frac{1}{19}\).
Flip the fraction (negate the log) and exponentiate.
Solve for \(N\).

keyPoints.note: Separate variables; the given partial fractions make the N-integral two logs.

steps.explain: The population tripled in the first year: \(N=3\times500=1500\) at \(t=1\).
Rearrange.
Take logs.

parts.answer: Tripled in the first year: N = 1500 at t = 1. \(1500=\frac{10000}{1+19e^{-10000k}}\Rightarrow1+19e^{-10000k}=\frac{20}{3}\Rightarrow e^{-10000k}=\frac{17}{57}\Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{10000}\ln\frac{57}{17}\).

keyPoints.note: Use N = 1500 (three times 500) at t = 1.

parts.stem: Correct to the nearest month, how long will it take for the fish population in the lake to reach 7000 fish?
parts.hint: Use e^(−10000k) = 17/57, set N = 7000 and solve for t, then convert years to months.

steps.explain: Take logs.
Convert to months.

keyPoints.note: Substitute N = 7000 and use e^(−10000k) = 17/57 from (ii).

questions.stem: Soup cools according to \(T=21+75e^{-kt}\), where t is minutes after removal from the stove. It is 87°C after 5 minutes. How much longer after that measurement must Miriam wait for it to reach 70°C?
questions.hint: Use the 87°C measurement to find k; then solve for the total time when T=70°C and subtract 5 minutes.

keyPoints.note: Substitute this measurement to determine the cooling constant k.
Find the total time to 70°C, then subtract the 5 minutes already elapsed.

steps.explain: Use \(T(5)=87\) to find k.
Solve the model for the total time when T=70.
Subtract the first five minutes already elapsed.

questions.stem:
Metal Fatigue is a phenomenon where a piece of steel will fail when repeatedly subjected to force \(F\). The endurance limit is the force below which the steel will not break even if subjected to an infinite number of application of that force. Let the number of applications be \(n\).

The force and the number of applications are related by the differential equation \(\frac{dF}{dn}=-k(F-F_0)\) where \(k\) and \(F_0\) are constants.

parts.stem: Show that \(F=275e^{-k(n-1)}+F_0\) is a solution to the differential equation.
parts.hint: Differentiate and replace 275e^(−k(n−1)) by F − F₀.

steps.explain: Differentiate with respect to \(n\).
From the given \(F\), \(275e^{-k(n-1)}=F-F_0\).

keyPoints.note: Differentiate F with respect to n and write the result in terms of F.

parts.stem: If \(F=350\) when \(n=1\), find the value of \(F_0\).

steps.explain: At \(n=1\) the exponent is 0.

keyPoints.note: Substitute n = 1: e^(−k·0) = 1.

parts.stem: Find the exact value of \(k\) if \(F=80\) when \(n=200\).

steps.explain: Substitute with \(F_0=75\).
Take logs.

keyPoints.note: n = 200 gives exponent −k(199). Use F₀ = 75.

steps.explain: The endurance limit is what \(F\) approaches as \(n\to\infty\). Since \(k\gt0\), \(e^{-k(n-1)}\to0\).

keyPoints.note: As n → ∞ the exponential term vanishes.

questions.stem: A piece of hot metal is placed in a room with a surrounding air temperature of 15°C and allowed to cool. It loses heat according to Newton's law of cooling: \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-A)\), where \(T\) is the temperature of the metal in degrees Celsius at time \(t\) minutes, \(A\) is the surrounding air temperature and \(k\) is a positive constant. After 5 minutes the temperature of the metal is 75°C, and after a further 3 minutes it is 45°C. Solve the differential equation, expressing your answer in the form \(T=f(t)\) and giving all constants in exact form.
questions.hint: The solution of Newton's law is \(T=A+Ce^{-kt}\) with \(A=15\). Use the two data points to find \(C\) and \(k\).

steps.explain: General solution with \(A=15\).
Divide the equations to find \(k\).
Find \(C\).
Substitute.

keyPoints.note: General solution \(T=A+Ce^{-kt}\), then use the two readings.

steps.explain: Test the equations at \(t=0\), where \(e^{-k\cdot 0}=e^{0}=1\).
Only B and D give 3000 at \(t=0\). Now the long-term value: as \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-kt}\to 0\) (for \(k>0\)).
B starts at 3000 and levels off at 1500 ✓. The \(+1500e^{-kt}\) term is positive and shrinks, so \(P\) decreases from above toward 1500, just like the graph.
Option A starts at 1500 and goes to 0; option C starts at 1500 and increases toward 3000; option D heads to 4500 (it increases).
So the correct choice is option B.

questions.stem: \(N\) is the number of finches at time \(t\) years, with \(N=1500+2000e^{-kt}\) and \(k=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{20}{13}\right)\approx 0.2154\). How long will it take for the population to drop to 2100, correct to one decimal place?
questions.hint: Substitute \(N=2100\), isolate \(e^{-kt}\), then take the natural log and divide by \(-k\).

steps.explain: Subtract 1500, then divide by 2000: \(\dfrac{600}{2000}=0.3\).
Take natural logs: \(\ln e^{-kt}=-kt\).
Solve for \(t\): divide by \(-k\). Use the exact value \(k=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{20}{13}\).
Calculate and round to 1 decimal place.
